claim: Perceptual learning is often orientation and location specific.
source: Perceptual learning is often orientation and location specific, which may indicate neuronal plasticity in early visual areas.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Orientation and location specificity of perceptual learning may indicate neuronal plasticity in early visual areas.
source: Perceptual learning is often orientation and location specific, which may indicate neuronal plasticity in early visual areas.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation commonly proposed in the field.

claim: Learning specificity diminishes with additional exposure of the transfer orientation or location via irrelevant tasks.
source: However, learning specificity diminishes with additional exposure of the transfer orientation or location via irrelevant tasks, suggesting that the specificity is related to untrained conditions, likely because neurons representing untrained conditions are neither bottom-up stimulated nor top-down attended during training.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous double training studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Learning specificity is related to untrained conditions because neurons representing untrained conditions are neither bottom-up stimulated nor top-down attended during training.
source: However, learning specificity diminishes with additional exposure of the transfer orientation or location via irrelevant tasks, suggesting that the specificity is related to untrained conditions, likely because neurons representing untrained conditions are neither bottom-up stimulated nor top-down attended during training.
evidence: This is the authors' hypothesis based on their previous findings.

claim: Either bottom-up or top-down influences enabled significant transfer of orientation and Vernier discrimination learning.
source: We found that either bottom-up or top-down influences enabled significant transfer of orientation and Vernier discrimination learning.
evidence: This is the main finding of the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: Learning specificity may result from under-activations of untrained visual neurons due to insufficient bottom-up stimulation and/or top-down attention during training.
source: These results suggest that learning specificity may result from under-activations of untrained visual neurons due to insufficient bottom-up stimulation and/or top-down attention during training.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their experimental findings.

claim: High-level perceptual learning may not functionally connect to neurons representing untrained conditions for learning transfer.
source: High-level perceptual learning thus may not functionally connect to these neurons for learning transfer.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing that activation of untrained neurons enables transfer.

claim: Visual perceptual learning is the process in which observers improve their discrimination of fine differences of basic visual features through practice.
source: Visual perceptual learning is the process in which the observers improve their discrimination of fine differences of basic visual features, such as contrast, orientation, motion direction, etc., through practice.
evidence: This is a standard definition in the field.

claim: Visual perceptual learning has been regarded as a distinct format of learning because it is specific to the orientation and retinal location of the trained stimulus.
source: For several decades visual perceptual learning has been regarded as a distinct format of learning because it is specific to the orientation and retinal location of the trained stimulus (Schoups et al., 1995; Ahissar and Hochstein, 1997; Shiu and Pashler, 1992; Dosher and Lu, 1998; Poggio et al., 1992; Fiorentini and Berardi, 1980; Yu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: Learning specificity has inspired theories that interpret visual perceptual learning as a result of training induced neural plasticity in the early visual areas.
source: Such learning specificity has inspired theories that interpret visual perceptual learning as a result of training induced neural plasticity in the early visual areas (Schoups et al., 1995; Karni and Sagi, 1991; Teich and Qian, 2003; Bejjanki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work in the field.

claim: Training could sharpen neuronal orientation tuning in the primary visual cortex (V1), so that neurons become more sensitive to fine changes of orientation differences.
source: For example, it has been proposed that training could sharpen neuronal orientation tuning in the primary visual cortex (V1), so that neurons become more sensitive to the fine changes of orientation differences (Teich and Qian, 2003; Schoups et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations.

claim: Reweighting theories propose that training may not change the tuning properties of sensory neurons, but rather the inputs from activated neurons are reweighted through training to improve readout at a later decision stage.
source: These theories propose that training may not change the tuning properties of sensory neurons. Rather, the inputs from activated neurons are reweighted through training to improve readout at a later decision stage.
evidence: This is a description of reweighting theories supported by citations.

claim: Motion direction learning in monkeys is correlated with changes in motion-driven responses of neurons in the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) but not with changes of neurons in the medial temporal area (MT).
source: For example, motion direction learning in monkeys is correlated with changes in motion-driven responses of neurons in the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) that is related to the transformation of motion information into decisions (saccadic choices), but not with changes of neurons in the medial temporal area (MT) that represents motion direction signals (Law and Gold, 2008).
evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited neurophysiological study.

claim: Visual perceptual learning of various tasks can transfer significantly, and often completely, to new orientations or locations in double training studies.
source: However, in a series of 'double training' studies we demonstrated that visual perceptual learning of various tasks can transfer significantly, and often completely, to new orientations or locations (Xiao et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2012, 2014; Zhang et al., 2010, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous published studies.

claim: Perceptual learning of foveal orientation discrimination initially shows little transfer to an orthogonal orientation.
source: For example, perceptual learning of foveal orientation discrimination (e.g., which of two consecutively presented gratings is more clockwise-tilted?) initially shows little transfer to an orthogonal orientation.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: If observers are exposed to an orthogonal orientation via an irrelevant contrast discrimination task, orientation learning transfers completely to the orthogonal orientation.
source: However, if the observers are exposed to an orthogonal orientation via an irrelevant contrast discrimination task (e.g., which of two gratings has higher contrast?), learning transfers completely to the orthogonal orientation (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a specific finding from a cited study by the authors.

claim: Perceptual learning of Vernier discrimination can transfer significantly and often completely to a new retinal location when observers are additionally exposed to the transfer location via an irrelevant contrast or orientation discrimination task.
source: Similarly, perceptual learning of Vernier discrimination (e.g., whether a lower grating is placed to the left or right of an upper grating) can also transfer significantly and often completely to a new retinal location when the observers are additionally exposed to the transfer location via an irrelevant contrast or orientation discrimination task (Wang et al., 2012, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous published studies.

claim: Visual perceptual learning is mainly a high-level rule-based learning process that occurs beyond the retinotopic and orientation selective visual areas.
source: First, visual perceptual learning is mainly a high-level rule-based learning process that occurs beyond the retinotopic and orientation selective visual areas, so that learning is in principle transferrable to untrained conditions (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is the authors' theoretical interpretation based on their previous findings.

claim: Learning is in principle transferrable to untrained conditions.
source: First, visual perceptual learning is mainly a high-level rule-based learning process that occurs beyond the retinotopic and orientation selective visual areas, so that learning is in principle transferrable to untrained conditions (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the high-level nature of perceptual learning.

claim: Learning specificity may be related to the untrained conditions, rather than the trained conditions.
source: Second, learning specificity may be related to the untrained conditions, rather than the trained conditions as the field has been assuming (i.e., plasticity with the trained early visual cortical neurons or reweighting of the inputs from these neurons).
evidence: This is the authors' novel theoretical proposal based on their findings.

claim: During training at a specific orientation or location, most mental resources are devoted to the trained stimuli.
source: During training at a specific orientation or location in a typical visual perceptual learning experiment, most mental resources are devoted to the trained stimuli.
evidence: This is a reasonable inference about attentional allocation during training.

claim: The untrained orientations and locations, and thus the visual neurons representing these orientations and locations, are neither bottom-up stimulated nor top-down attended during training.
source: As a result the untrained orientations and locations, and thus the visual neurons representing these orientations and locations, are neither bottom-up stimulated nor top-down attended during training.
evidence: This is inferred from the attentional focus on trained conditions.

claim: Insufficient bottom-up stimulation of, and/or top-down attention to, the untrained conditions are responsible for the orientation and location specificity.
source: We thus suspect that this insufficient bottom-up stimulation of, and/or top-down attention to, the untrained conditions are responsible for the orientation and location specificity.
evidence: This is the authors' hypothesis to be tested in the study.

claim: Because visual neurons representing untrained conditions are not properly activated, high-level perceptual learning may not be able to functionally connect to these neurons for learning transfer.
source: In other words, because visual neurons representing untrained conditions are not properly activated as a result, high-level perceptual learning may not be able to functionally connect to these neurons for learning transfer.
evidence: This is the authors' mechanistic hypothesis.

claim: Previous double training experiments are unable to separately identify the potential bottom-up and/or top-down contributions because suprathreshold stimuli are used in the secondary exposure task.
source: Our previous double training experiments are unable to separately identify the potential bottom-up and/or top-down contributions because suprathreshold stimuli are used in the secondary exposure task.
evidence: This is a limitation of previous methods acknowledged by the authors.

claim: A continuous flash suppression (CFS) technique was applied to suppress the exposure stimulus into sub-consciousness.
source: In the current study we applied a continuous flash suppression (CFS) technique (Tsuchiya and Koch, 2005) to suppress the exposure stimulus into sub-consciousness (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Five sessions of orientation discrimination training reduced thresholds by 42.1 ± 3.4% at the trained orientation.
source: The observers practiced orientation discrimination with a foveal Gabor stimulus at 36° or 126° for 5 daily sessions, which reduced the thresholds by 42.1 ± 3.4% (mean ± se; t9 = 12.46, p<0.001, 95% CI = 34.4% to 49.7%, Cohen's d = 3.94; two-tailed paired t-test in this and later analyses when the significance of the improvement was tested) at the trained orientation (Figure 1a and g).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: Training only reduced the orientation thresholds at the untrained orthogonal orientation by 11.8 ± 4.6%.
source: Training only reduced the orientation thresholds with the same stimulus at the untrained orthogonal orientation by 11.8 ± 4.6% (t9 = 2.56, p = 0.030, 95% CI = 1.4% to 22.2%, Cohen's d = 0.81).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: The improvement was significantly lower at the untrained orientation than at the trained orientation in the baseline condition.
source: The improvement was significantly lower at the untrained orientation than at the trained orientation (t9 = 6.39, p<0.001, 95% CI = 19.56% to 40.98%, Cohen's d = 2.02).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental results.

claim: The transfer index in the baseline condition was 0.25 ± 0.10, indicating that learning is mostly orientation specific.
source: Here TI = 0.25 ± 0.10 (t9 = 2.47, p = 0.036, 95% CI = 0.02 to 0.49, Cohen's d = 0.78; Figure 1h), indicating that learning is mostly orientation specific.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure derived from experimental data.

claim: Five sessions of practice with orientation training and bottom-up stimulation reduced orientation discrimination thresholds at the trained orientation by 50.6 ± 6.0%.
source: Five sessions of practice reduced the orientation discrimination thresholds at the trained orientation significantly by 50.6 ± 6.0% (t9 = 8.87, p<0.001, 95% CI = 35.9% to 60.5%, Cohen's d = 2.80), as well as at the untrained but bottom-up stimulated orthogonal orientation by 33.7 ± 4.6% (t9 = 7.33, p<0.001, 95% CI = 23.3% to 44.1%, Cohen's d = 2.32) (Figure 1d and g).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: Five sessions of practice with orientation training and bottom-up stimulation reduced orientation discrimination thresholds at the untrained but bottom-up stimulated orthogonal orientation by 33.7 ± 4.6%.
source: Five sessions of practice reduced the orientation discrimination thresholds at the trained orientation significantly by 50.6 ± 6.0% (t9 = 8.87, p<0.001, 95% CI = 35.9% to 60.5%, Cohen's d = 2.80), as well as at the untrained but bottom-up stimulated orthogonal orientation by 33.7 ± 4.6% (t9 = 7.33, p<0.001, 95% CI = 23.3% to 44.1%, Cohen's d = 2.32) (Figure 1d and g).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant difference between the improvements at the trained and transfer orientations with bottom-up stimulation.
source: There was still a significant difference between the two improvements (t9 = 3.84, p = 0.004, 95% CI = 5.9% to 23.0%, Cohen's d = 1.21), and the transfer index TI = 0.72 ± 0.08 (t9 = 9.09, p<0.001, 95% CI = 0.54 to 0.90, Cohen's d = 2.87; Figure 1h), indicating substantial but incomplete learning transfer.
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental results.

claim: The transfer index with bottom-up stimulation was 0.72 ± 0.08, indicating substantial but incomplete learning transfer.
source: There was still a significant difference between the two improvements (t9 = 3.84, p = 0.004, 95% CI = 5.9% to 23.0%, Cohen's d = 1.21), and the transfer index TI = 0.72 ± 0.08 (t9 = 9.09, p<0.001, 95% CI = 0.54 to 0.90, Cohen's d = 2.87; Figure 1h), indicating substantial but incomplete learning transfer.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure derived from experimental data.

claim: Bottom-up stimulation alone changed the orientation discrimination thresholds at the stimulated orientation insignificantly by 9.7 ± 4.3%.
source: Eight new observers received equal amount of bottom-up stimulation of the orthogonal transfer orientation without practicing the orientation discrimination task. The bottom-up stimulation changed the orientation discrimination thresholds at the stimulated orientation insignificantly by 9.7 ± 4.3% (t7 = 2.25, p = 0.06, 95% CI = -0.05% to 19.9%, Cohen's d = 0.85, Figure 1e and g).
evidence: This is a control experiment result with statistical analysis.

claim: The improvement at the untrained orthogonal orientation did not result from the bottom-up stimulation alone.
source: A control experiment indicated that the improvement at the untrained orthogonal orientation did not result from the bottom-up stimulation alone.
evidence: This is concluded from the control experiment data.

claim: Training with noise-only (no orthogonal Gabor) reduced orientation thresholds significantly by 46.7 ± 3.4%.
source: Again training reduced orientation thresholds significantly by 46.7 ± 3.4% (t9 = 13.92, p<0.001, 95% CI = 39.1% to 54.3%, Cohen's d = 4.40) in ten observers (Figure 1f and g).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: No significant threshold improvement was evident at the orthogonal transfer orientation with training plus noise-only (13.4 ± 8.8%).
source: However, no significant threshold improvement was evident at the orthogonal transfer orientation (13.4 ± 8.8%, t9 = 1.53, p = 0.16, 95% CI = -6.5% to 33.2%, Cohen's d = 0.51), which was significantly lower than the improvement at the trained orientation (t9 = 4.13, p = 0.003, 95% CI = 15.1% to 51.6%, Cohen's d = 1.44).
evidence: This is a control experiment result with statistical analysis.

claim: The transfer index in the training plus noise-only condition was 0.24 ± 0.24.
source: The TI = 0.24 ± 0.24 in this condition (t9 = 0.99, p = 0.35, 95% CI = -0.31 to 0.79, Cohen's d = 0.31; Figure 1h).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure derived from experimental data.

claim: The training plus bottom-up stimulation condition had significantly more transfer than the baseline condition.
source: Post-hoc Dunn's multiple comparison indicated that the training plus bottom-up stimulation condition had significantly more transfer than the baseline condition (p = 0.004 without correction; p = 0.011 with correction) and the training plus noise-only condition (p = 0.022 without correction or 0.067 with correction).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental conditions.

claim: There was no significant difference of the transfer effects between the training plus noise-only condition and the baseline condition.
source: There was no significant difference of the transfer effects between the training plus noise-only condition and the baseline condition (p = 0.54 without correction or 1.00 with correction).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental conditions.

claim: Bottom-up stimulation of the transfer orientation can enable substantial but partial transfer of orientation learning.
source: There results together suggest that bottom-up stimulation of the transfer orientation can enable substantial but partial transfer of orientation learning.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results.

claim: High-level perceptual learning may functionally connect to salient orientation signals for learning transfer even if these signals are subconscious.
source: Moreover, high-level perceptual learning may functionally connect to salient orientation signals for learning transfer even if these signals are subconscious.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that subconscious bottom-up stimulation enables transfer.

claim: Training with top-down attention to the transfer orientation improved orientation thresholds at the trained orientation by 39.5 ± 3.5%.
source: Training and top-down attention to the transfer orientation improved orientation thresholds at the trained orientation by 39.5 ± 3.5% (t9 = 11.21, p<0.001, 95% CI = 31.5% to 47.4%, Cohen's d = 3.54) in ten observers (Figure 2b and d).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: Training with top-down attention to the transfer orientation improved thresholds at the orthogonal orientation by 29.0 ± 3.4%.
source: The threshold reduction at the orthogonal orientation was also significant (29.0 ± 3.4%, t9 = 8.45, p<0.001, 95% CI = 21.3% to 36.8%, Cohen's d = 2.67), indicating the effectiveness of top-down orientation attention in enabling learning transfer.
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: Top-down orientation attention is effective in enabling learning transfer.
source: The threshold reduction at the orthogonal orientation was also significant (29.0 ± 3.4%, t9 = 8.45, p<0.001, 95% CI = 21.3% to 36.8%, Cohen's d = 2.67), indicating the effectiveness of top-down orientation attention in enabling learning transfer.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results.

claim: The improvement at the untrained orientation was significantly lower than that at the trained orientation with top-down attention.
source: The improvement at the untrained orientation was significantly lower than that at the trained orientation (t9 = 2.53, p = 0.032, 95% CI = 1.1% to 19.8%, Cohen's d = 0.80), and the transfer index was 0.77 ± 0.10 (t9 = 7.86, p<0.001, 95% CI = 0.55 to 1, Cohen's d = 2.48; Figure 2e), suggesting substantial but partial learning transfer.
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental results.

claim: The transfer index with top-down attention was 0.77 ± 0.10, suggesting substantial but partial learning transfer.
source: The improvement at the untrained orientation was significantly lower than that at the trained orientation (t9 = 2.53, p = 0.032, 95% CI = 1.1% to 19.8%, Cohen's d = 0.80), and the transfer index was 0.77 ± 0.10 (t9 = 7.86, p<0.001, 95% CI = 0.55 to 1, Cohen's d = 2.48; Figure 2e), suggesting substantial but partial learning transfer.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure derived from experimental data.

claim: Without actual training of orientation discrimination, top-down attention to the transfer orientation alone led to an insignificant reduction of orientation threshold at the transfer orientation (8.0 ± 4.4%).
source: A control experiment with eight observers indicated that, without actual training of orientation discrimination, top-down attention to the transfer orientation alone led to an insignificant reduction of orientation threshold at the transfer orientation (8.0 ± 4.4%, t7 = 1.81, p = 0.11, 95% CI = -2.4% to 18.4%, Cohen's d = 0.64) (Figure 2c and d).
evidence: This is a control experiment result with statistical analysis.

claim: Top-down attention alone did not improve orientation discrimination at the transfer orientation.
source: This control ruled out the possibility that top-down attention alone improved orientation discrimination at the transfer orientation.
evidence: This is concluded from the control experiment data.

claim: The training plus top-down attention condition had significantly more transfer than the baseline condition.
source: Post-hoc Dunn's multiple comparison indicated that the training plus top-down attention condition had significantly more transfer than the baseline condition (p = 0.003 without correction; p = 0.008 with correction) and the training plus noise-only condition (p = 0.019 without correction or 0.058 with correction).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental conditions.

claim: Top-down attention, like bottom-up stimulation, is sufficient to enable substantial but partial learning transfer to the untrained orthogonal orientation.
source: These results indicate that top-down attention, like bottom-up stimulation, is sufficient to enable substantial but partial learning transfer to the untrained orthogonal orientation.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results.

claim: Training with combined bottom-up stimulation and top-down attention significantly reduced orientation thresholds at the trained orientation by 45.1 ± 5.4%.
source: Training significantly reduced the orientation thresholds at both the trained orientation (45.1 ± 5.4%, t8 = 8.25, p<0.001, 95% CI = 32.5% to 57.8%, Cohen's d = 2.49) and the orthogonal transfer orientation (39.0 ± 4.3%, t8 = 9.00, p<0.001, 95% CI = 29.0% to 49.0%, Cohen's d = 2.38) in nine observers (Figure 3b–d).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: Training with combined bottom-up stimulation and top-down attention significantly reduced orientation thresholds at the orthogonal transfer orientation by 39.0 ± 4.3%.
source: Training significantly reduced the orientation thresholds at both the trained orientation (45.1 ± 5.4%, t8 = 8.25, p<0.001, 95% CI = 32.5% to 57.8%, Cohen's d = 2.49) and the orthogonal transfer orientation (39.0 ± 4.3%, t8 = 9.00, p<0.001, 95% CI = 29.0% to 49.0%, Cohen's d = 2.38) in nine observers (Figure 3b–d).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference between the improvements at the trained and transfer orientations with combined bottom-up and top-down influences.
source: There was no significant difference between the two improvements (t8 = 1.20, p = 0.26, 95% CI = -5.7% to 18.0%, Cohen's d = 0.40).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental results.

claim: The transfer index with combined bottom-up and top-down influences was 0.94 ± 0.12, indicating nearly complete learning transfer to the untrained orthogonal orientation.
source: The transfer index was 0.94 ± 0.12 (t8 = 7.78, p<0.001, 95% CI = 0.66 to 1.22, Cohen's d = 2.59; Figure 3e), indicating nearly complete learning transfer to the untrained orthogonal orientation.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure derived from experimental data.

claim: The combined bottom-up stimulation and top-down attention without actual orientation training only led to a small threshold improvement at the exposed orientation (14.6 ± 4.4%).
source: In a control experiment, the combined bottom-up stimulation and top-down attention without actual orientation training only led to a small threshold improvement at the exposed orientation (14.6 ± 4.4%, t7 = 3.31, p=0.013, 95% CI = 4.2% to 25.1%, Cohen's d = 1.17) (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This is a control experiment result with statistical analysis.

claim: The improvement in the control condition was significantly lower than that with orientation training.
source: The improvement was significantly lower than that in Figure 3b with orientation training (t15 = 3.93, p=0.001, 95% CI = 11.2% to 37.6%, Cohen's d = 1.91, two-tailed unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between experimental and control conditions.

claim: The combined bottom-up stimulation and top-down attention to the transfer orientation alone did not cause the substantial improvement of orientation discrimination.
source: This control ruled out the possibility that the combined bottom-up stimulation and top-down attention to the transfer orientation alone caused the substantial improvement of orientation discrimination shown in Figure 3b.
evidence: This is concluded from the control experiment data.

claim: The Gabor/C judgments were near chance (0.80) after some initial increase, suggesting effective suppression of stimulus perceptions with continuous flashing noise.
source: In Figure 3b and c the Gabor/C judgments were near chance (0.80) after some initial increase, suggesting effective suppression of stimulus perceptions with continuous flashing noise.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The training plus combined bottom-up and top-down condition had significantly more transfer than the baseline condition.
source: Post-hoc Dunn's multiple comparison indicated that the training plus combined bottom-up and top-down condition had significantly more transfer than the baseline condition (p = 0.001 without correction; p = 0.003 with correction) and the training plus noise-only condition (p = 0.007 without correction or 0.022 with correction).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental conditions.

claim: Observers showed a chance-level accuracy of 0.51 ± 0.01 in detecting the sub-conscious Gabor at the transfer orientation.
source: Each observer was presented a sub-conscious Gabor at the transfer orientation in half the trials with flashing noise presented to the other eye (50 trials per block for four blocks). In the other half trials a blank screen was presented. The result showed a chance-level accuracy at 0.51 ± 0.01.
evidence: This is a direct experimental result confirming effective suppression.

claim: The transfer results in Figures 1-3 were not contaminated by the leakage of the Gabor perception.
source: Therefore, the transfer results in Figure 1–3 were not contaminated by the leakage of the Gabor perception.
evidence: This is concluded from the chance-level detection data.

claim: Vernier learning at one visual quadrant location showed zero transfer to a diagonal location in a previous study.
source: In our previous study (Wang et al., 2014) that used the same stimulus configuration as here in Figure 4, Vernier learning at one visual quadrant location showed zero transfer to a diagonal location, with the transfer index TI = -0.1 ± 0.16.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous published study.

claim: Additional training at the transfer location with an orientation discrimination task successfully enabled Vernier learning transfer (TI = 0.98 ± 0.22).
source: However, additional training at the transfer location with an orientation discrimination task successfully enabled Vernier learning transfer (TI = 0.98 ± 0.22).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous published study.

claim: Vernier training with simultaneous subconscious bottom-up stimulation of the diagonal transfer location reduced Vernier thresholds by 32.4% ± 4.3% at the trained location.
source: Eight observers received five sessions of Vernier training and simultaneous subconscious bottom-up stimulation of the diagonal transfer location. This procedure reduced Vernier thresholds by 32.4% ± 4.3% (t7 = 7.54, p<0.001, 95% CI = 22.2% to 42.5%, Cohen's d = 2.32) at the trained location, as well as by 35.3% ± 6.4% (t7 = 5.53, p<0.001, 95% CI = 20.2% to 50.4%, Cohen's d = 1.95) at the transfer location (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: Vernier training with simultaneous subconscious bottom-up stimulation of the diagonal transfer location reduced Vernier thresholds by 35.3% ± 6.4% at the transfer location.
source: Eight observers received five sessions of Vernier training and simultaneous subconscious bottom-up stimulation of the diagonal transfer location. This procedure reduced Vernier thresholds by 32.4% ± 4.3% (t7 = 7.54, p<0.001, 95% CI = 22.2% to 42.5%, Cohen's d = 2.32) at the trained location, as well as by 35.3% ± 6.4% (t7 = 5.53, p<0.001, 95% CI = 20.2% to 50.4%, Cohen's d = 1.95) at the transfer location (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: The improvements at the trained and transfer locations were comparable with bottom-up stimulation.
source: The two improvements were comparable (t7 = 0.54, p = 0.60, 95% CI = −15.6% to 9.8%, Cohen's d = 0.19).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental results.

claim: The transfer index for Vernier learning with bottom-up stimulation was 1.13 ± 0.17, indicating complete transfer of Vernier learning.
source: The TI = 1.13 ± 0.17 (t7 = 6.54, p<0.001, 95% CI = 0.72 to 1.55, Cohen's d = 2.31; Figure 4f), indicating complete transfer of Vernier learning.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure derived from experimental data.

claim: Mere bottom-up stimulation of the diagonal location without Vernier training produced insignificant change of Vernier performance at the stimulated location (4.1 ± 9.1%).
source: Without Vernier training (eight observers in a control condition instead reported the red/green color of a peripheral dot at the original Vernier stimulus location), mere bottom-up stimulation of the diagonal location produced insignificant change of Vernier performance at the stimulated location (4.1 ± 9.1%, t7 = 0.45, p = 0.67, 95% CI = −17.5% to 25.7%, Cohen's d = 0.16) (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a control experiment result with statistical analysis.

claim: Vernier learning transfer was not caused by the bottom-up stimulation alone.
source: This learning transfer was not caused by the bottom-up stimulation alone.
evidence: This is concluded from the control experiment data.

claim: Training without the horizontal Gabor at the transfer location reduced Vernier thresholds at the trained location by 32.3 ± 3.4%.
source: The training reduced Vernier thresholds in eight new observers at the trained location by 32.3 ± 3.4% (t7 = 9.42, p<0.001, 95% CI = 24.2% to 40.5%, Cohen's d = 3.33) (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: Training without the horizontal Gabor at the transfer location reduced Vernier thresholds at the transfer location insignificantly by 6.0 ± 4.3%.
source: However, training reduced Vernier thresholds at the transfer location insignificantly by 6.0 ± 4.3% (t7 = 1.40, p = 0.21, 95% CI = −4.1% to 16.1%, Cohen's d = 0.49).
evidence: This is a control experiment result with statistical analysis.

claim: The improvement was significantly lower at the transfer location than at the trained location without the Gabor stimulus.
source: The improvement was significantly lower at the transfer location than at the trained location (t7 = 8.01, p<0.001, 95% CI = 18.6% to 34.2%, Cohen's d = 2.83).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental results.

claim: The transfer index without the Gabor stimulus was 0.13 ± 0.11.
source: The transfer index TI = 0.13 ± 0.11 (t7 = 1.16, p = 0.28, 95% CI = −13.5% to 39.7%, Cohen's d = 0.41; Figure 4f).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure derived from experimental data.

claim: Bottom-up stimulation of the untrained location was necessary as well as sufficient for the complete learning transfer.
source: The above results together indicated that bottom-up stimulation of the untrained location was indeed necessary as well as sufficient for the complete learning transfer shown in Figure 4b.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing the experimental and control conditions.

claim: Vernier training with top-down attention to the transfer location improved Vernier thresholds at the trained location by 28.4 ± 4.0%.
source: The Vernier training and top-down attention to the transfer location improved Vernier thresholds at the trained location by 28.4 ± 4.0% (t7 = 6.86, p<0.001, 95% CI = 18.6% to 38.2%, Cohen's d = 2.43), as well as at the transfer location by 28.9 ± 4.9% (t7 = 6.42, p<0.001, 95% CI = 18.3% to 40.0%, Cohen's d = 2.27) (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: Vernier training with top-down attention to the transfer location improved Vernier thresholds at the transfer location by 28.9 ± 4.9%.
source: The Vernier training and top-down attention to the transfer location improved Vernier thresholds at the trained location by 28.4 ± 4.0% (t7 = 6.86, p<0.001, 95% CI = 18.6% to 38.2%, Cohen's d = 2.43), as well as at the transfer location by 28.9 ± 4.9% (t7 = 6.42, p<0.001, 95% CI = 18.3% to 40.0%, Cohen's d = 2.27) (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result with statistical analysis.

claim: The improvements at the trained and transfer locations were nearly identical with top-down attention.
source: The two improvements were nearly identical (t7 = 0.22, p = 0.83, 95% CI = −5.3% to 6.4%, Cohen's d = 0.08), and the TI = 1.04 ± 0.08 (t7 = 11.80, p<0.001, 95% CI = 0.83 to 1.25, Cohen's d = 4.17; Figure 5e), indicating complete learning transfer.
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental results.

claim: The transfer index for Vernier learning with top-down attention was 1.04 ± 0.08, indicating complete learning transfer.
source: The two improvements were nearly identical (t7 = 0.22, p = 0.83, 95% CI = −5.3% to 6.4%, Cohen's d = 0.08), and the TI = 1.04 ± 0.08 (t7 = 11.80, p<0.001, 95% CI = 0.83 to 1.25, Cohen's d = 4.17; Figure 5e), indicating complete learning transfer.
evidence: This is a quantitative measure derived from experimental data.

claim: Top-down attention was necessary for the Vernier learning transfer.
source: The learning transfer was greater than that in the training plus noise-only condition in Figure 4d when the transfer indices were compared (p<0.001, independent-samples Mann-Whitney U test), suggesting that top-down attention was necessary for the learning transfer.
evidence: This is concluded from statistical comparison of conditions.

claim: Top-down attention trials only (without Vernier training) failed to improve the Vernier threshold at the transfer location (-1.1 ± 6.1%).
source: In addition, a control condition with top-down attention trials only (without Vernier training) failed to improve the Vernier threshold at the transfer location (-1.1 ± 6.1%, t7 = −0.19, p =0.85, 95% CI = −14.3% to 12.2%, Cohen's d = 0.07) (Figure 5c), ruling out the possibility that the learning transfer was a result of top-down attention alone.
evidence: This is a control experiment result with statistical analysis.

claim: The learning transfer was not a result of top-down attention alone.
source: In addition, a control condition with top-down attention trials only (without Vernier training) failed to improve the Vernier threshold at the transfer location (-1.1 ± 6.1%, t7 = −0.19, p =0.85, 95% CI = −14.3% to 12.2%, Cohen's d = 0.07) (Figure 5c), ruling out the possibility that the learning transfer was a result of top-down attention alone.
evidence: This is concluded from the control experiment data.

claim: Top-down spatial attention to the transfer location is sufficient to enable complete transfer of Vernier learning.
source: The results in Figure 5 together indicated that, like bottom-up stimulation, top-down spatial attention to the transfer location is also sufficient to enable complete transfer of Vernier learning.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results.

claim: The mean Gabor detection rate at the transfer location was 0.49 ± 0.01, indicating effective suppression.
source: The mean report rate was 0.49 ± 0.01.
evidence: This is a direct experimental result confirming effective suppression.

claim: The results in Figures 4 and 5 were not contaminated by the observers' likely perception of the Gabor stimulus at the transfer location.
source: Therefore, the results in Figures 4,5 were not contaminated by the observers' likely perception of the Gabor stimulus at the transfer location.
evidence: This is concluded from the chance-level detection data.

claim: It is the actions (or the absence of actions) with the untrained conditions that decide the learning specificity and transfer.
source: Here our results paint a completely opposite picture: It is the actions (or the absence of actions) with the untrained conditions that decide the learning specificity and transfer.
evidence: This is the authors' main theoretical conclusion from their experimental results.

claim: For orientation and location specificity, the absence of bottom-up stimulation of neurons representing the untrained conditions, as well as top-down attention to these neurons, prevent perceptual learning from transferring to untrained conditions.
source: We show that for orientation and location specificity, the absence of bottom-up stimulation of neurons representing the untrained conditions, as well as top-down attention to these neurons, prevent perceptual learning from transferring to untrained conditions.
evidence: This is the authors' main conclusion from their experimental results.

claim: Vernier learning and its transfer to an untrained hemisphere accompanies significant occipital P1-N1 changes when the Vernier task is performed at either the trained or the untrained location after training.
source: In one ERP study (Zhang et al., 2013), we discovered that Vernier learning and its transfer to an untrained hemisphere accompanies significant occipital P1-N1 changes when the Vernier task is performed at either the trained or the untrained location after training.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous ERP study.

claim: If Vernier learning does not transfer, the P1-N1 changes are limited to the trained location.
source: However, if learning does not transfer, as shown in about half the observers, the P1-N1 changes are limited to the trained location.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous ERP study.

claim: P1-N1 changes are possible indications of top-down connections between high-level Vernier learning and visual neurons at the trained location, as well as at untrained locations when learning transfers.
source: We interpret P1-N1 changes as possible indications of top-down connections between high-level Vernier learning and visual neurons at the trained location, as well as at untrained locations when learning transfers.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their ERP findings.

claim: Learning specificity is a result of absent functional connections.
source: We also interpret learning specificity as a result of absent functional connections.
evidence: This is the authors' theoretical interpretation.

claim: Both bottom-up stimulation of, and top-down attention to, untrained conditions may activate visual neurons representing the untrained conditions, so as to foster the connections to enable learning transfer.
source: Our current data suggest that both bottom-up stimulation of, and top-down attention to, untrained conditions may activate visual neurons representing the untrained conditions, so as to foster the connections to enable learning transfer.
evidence: This is the authors' mechanistic interpretation of their current findings.

claim: Orientation discrimination learning and its transfer to an untrained hemisphere accompanies significant occipital C1 changes when the orientation discrimination task is performed at the trained and untrained locations, respectively, after training.
source: In another ERP study (Zhang et al., 2015), we also found that orientation discrimination learning and its transfer to an untrained hemisphere accompanies significant occipital C1 changes when the orientation discrimination task is performed at the trained and untrained locations, respectively, after training (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous ERP study.

claim: C1 changes are not evident with an untrained shape-discrimination task or with passive viewing.
source: Such C1 changes are not evident with an untrained shape-discrimination task (Zhang et al., 2015) or with passive viewing (Bao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The functional connections are task specific.
source: These results further indicate that the functional connections are task specific, consistent with the observations that perceptual learning is task specific (Shiu and Pashler, 1992; Ahissar and Hochstein, 1993; Cong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from ERP findings and supported by citations.

claim: Perceptual learning is task specific.
source: These results further indicate that the functional connections are task specific, consistent with the observations that perceptual learning is task specific (Shiu and Pashler, 1992; Ahissar and Hochstein, 1993; Cong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: The generalized orientation discrimination learning is accompanied with task-specific enhancement of orientation-selective responses in the early visual areas including V1, V2 and V3.
source: The task-specific functional connections associated with learning and its transfer are also supported by fMRI evidence, in that the generalized orientation discrimination learning is accompanied with task-specific enhancement of orientation-selective responses in the early visual areas including V1, V2 and V3 (Byers and Serences, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited fMRI study.

claim: Orientation specificity is accompanied with refined representation of the trained orientation in early visual areas.
source: These results together may also explain fMRI results that orientation specificity is accompanied with refined representation of the trained orientation in early visual areas (Jehee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited fMRI study.

claim: Top-down modulation by high-level orientation learning may not reach the early cortical representations of untrained orientations as a result of absent functional connections.
source: This is because top-down modulation by high-level orientation learning may not reach the early cortical representations of untrained orientations as a result of absent functional connections.
evidence: This is the authors' explanation for fMRI findings based on their theory.

claim: When a near-threshold task is practiced, most brain resources are devoted to the training orientation and retinal location.
source: As we pointed out earlier, when a near-threshold task is practiced, most brain resources are devoted to the training orientation and retinal location.
evidence: This is a reasonable inference about resource allocation during training.

claim: Spatial attention could suppress other unattended locations even with no presence of competing stimuli.
source: At least in the case of location specificity, there is evidence that spatial attention could suppress other unattended locations even with no presence of competing stimuli (Smith et al., 2000; Shmuel et al., 2006), as is typical in a perceptual learning study.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Under-activations of neurons at untrained conditions could lead to missing functional connections of these neurons to high-level learning to prevent learning transfer.
source: We suspect that some or all of these factors could contribute to under-activations of neurons at untrained conditions, which in turn could lead to missing functional connections of these neurons to high-level learning to prevent learning transfer.
evidence: This is the authors' mechanistic hypothesis.

claim: The brain learns the rules of reweighting visual inputs to achieve better visual performance, and these rules are potentially applicable to new orientations and retinal locations.
source: Specifically, we suggest that visual perceptual learning is a high-level process. The brain learns the rules of reweighting visual inputs to achieve better visual performance, and these rules are potentially applicable to new orientations and retinal locations.
evidence: This is the authors' rule-based perceptual learning theory.

claim: Learning rules are conceptual, in that learning can transfer between physically distinct stimuli that are initially encoded by different neural mechanisms.
source: More recent evidence also suggests that these rules are conceptual, in that learning can transfer between physically distinct stimuli that are initially encoded by different neural mechanisms (e.g., between local and global orientations defined by gratings and symmetric dot patterns, or between first- and second-order motion directions) (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' recent work.

claim: Double training schemes function by providing bottom-up and top-down forces to activate untrained neurons, which in turn initiate functional connections for learning transfer.
source: These results also suggest that double training schemes function by providing bottom-up and top-down forces to activate untrained neurons, which in turn initiate functional connections for learning transfer.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of how double training works.

claim: A computational model explains how functional connections can be built with double training through off-task self-organization.
source: A recent computational model explains how such functional connections can be built with double training (Solgi et al., 2013). In the model, the secondary training task activates the untrained neurons, which could be recalled when the brain is off-task, so that high-level 'concept neurons' that have learned the task can connect to these untrained neurons in an off-task self-organization manner for learning transfer.
evidence: This is a description of a computational model from a cited study.

claim: The activations of untrained neurons due to unconsciousness stimulation, or top-down attention without actual stimulation, can be recalled off-task.
source: Apparently the activations of untrained neurons due to unconsciousness stimulation, or top-down attention without actual stimulation, can also be recalled off-task in the context of this computational account.
evidence: This is the authors' extension of the computational model to their findings.

claim: Peripheral Vernier training with simultaneous flashing of a Gabor at a diagonal location (without noise suppression) showed no evidence for learning transfer.
source: We once had observers practice a peripheral Vernier task identical to the current one, while flashing a Gabor simultaneously at a diagonal location (without noise suppression) for the purpose of stimulating neurons at this latter location (Wang et al., 2012). However, we found no evidence for learning transfer.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous study.

claim: A recent psychophysical study replicated the null-transfer results with simultaneous stimulus presentation.
source: A more recent psychophysical study also replicated the null-transfer results (Mastropasqua et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to another study.

claim: An earlier monkey-recording study reported that orientation discrimination learning does not transfer to a different location where a same grating stimulus is simultaneously presented.
source: Similarly, an earlier monkey-recording study (Schoups et al., 2001) reported that orientation discrimination learning does not transfer to a different location where a same grating stimulus is simultaneously presented.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited monkey study.

claim: Null-transfer effects with simultaneous stimulation may be caused by attentional competition, in that concentrated attention to the training location would suppress the high-contrast stimuli at a different location.
source: These null-transfer effects may be caused by attentional competition, in that concentrated attention to the training location would suppress the high-contrast stimuli at a different location (Watanabe et al., 2001).
evidence: This is the authors' explanation supported by a citation.

claim: The attentional suppression effect is avoided in double training when the primary training and the secondary training are performed in alternating blocks of trials.
source: The attentional suppression effect is avoided in double training when the primary training and the secondary training that stimulates the untrained location are performed in alternating blocks of trials (Xiao et al., 2008), or when the stimulation of the untrained locations is below awareness as in our current study.
evidence: This is the authors' explanation for why their methods work.

claim: Bottom-up stimulation of transfer location through one eye may create an input contrast in the eye-of-origin feature, which is very salient because it more strongly activates V1 neurons than the surrounding stimuli.
source: In the latter case the bottom-up stimulation of transfer location through one eye may create an input contrast in the eye-of-origin feature, and this contrast, although invisible perceptually, has been shown to be very salient because it more strongly activates V1 neurons than the surrounding stimuli (Zhaoping, 2008).
evidence: This is an explanation supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Training improves discrimination of a nearby feature that is task irrelevant and sub-threshold when the irrelevant feature is temporally paired with rewards with the trained task.
source: Watanabe and colleagues (Watanabe et al., 2001; Seitz and Watanabe, 2003) reported that training improves discrimination of a nearby feature that is task irrelevant and sub-threshold (to avoid attentional suppression), and that the learning occurs only when the irrelevant feature is temporally paired with rewards with the trained task.
evidence: This is a finding from cited studies on task-irrelevant perceptual learning.

claim: Task irrelevant perceptual learning (TIPL) results from interactions between spatially diffusive rewards and bottom-up exposure of the task irrelevant feature.
source: They explained this task irrelevant perceptual learning (TIPL) as a result of interactions between spatially diffusive rewards and bottom-up exposure of the task irrelevant feature (Seitz and Watanabe, 2005).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation from a cited study.

claim: Double-training enabled learning transfer is distinct from TIPL in that training and exposure do not require temporal pairing and spatial proximity of two stimuli.
source: First, unlike TIPL, the training and exposure do not require temporal pairing and spatial proximity of two stimuli. Indeed the training phase can precede the exposure phase with a time gap of up to 8 weeks (Zhang et al., 2010), and the training and exposure locations can be at diagonal quadrants of the visual field separated by 10 degrees (Wang et al., 2012), while double training is still effective.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' previous studies.

claim: Double-training enabled learning transfer is still task specific.
source: Second, our recent evidence suggests that double-training enabled learning transfer is still task specific (Cong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' recent work.

claim: Orientation discrimination learning cannot transfer to a contrast discrimination task using the same Gabor stimulus, even after observers receive additional exposure of the transfer task through easy trials in separate blocks of trials.
source: We found that orientation discrimination learning cannot transfer to a contrast discrimination task using the same Gabor stimulus, even after the observers receive additional exposure of the transfer task through easy trials in separate blocks of trials.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' recent work.

claim: One hundred and thirteen undergraduate students with normal or corrected-to-normal vision participated in this study.
source: One hundred and thirteen (113) undergraduate students with normal or corrected-to-normal vision participated in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: All participants were inexperienced in psychophysical observations and were naïve to the purpose of the study.
source: All were inexperienced in psychophysical observations and were naïve to the purpose of the study.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: This study was approved by the Peking University Institution Review Board.
source: This study was approved by the Peking University Institution Review Board.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.
